newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberians mass for presidential inauguration.
newsitem.headline: Liberians mass for presidential inauguration.

text.p: Thousands of people massed in Liberia's capital Monrovia on Saturday for the war-ravaged country's first presidential inauguration for over 12 years.
Invited guests from other African countries started arriving in the city on Friday to witness the installation of former warlord Charles Taylor as president.
About a dozen heads of state were arriving, among them Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha, Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and Laurent Kabila of Democratic Congo.
Officials in neighbouring Ivory Coast said President Henri Konan Bedie was heading a large Ivorian delegation.
President Bill Clinton on Friday announced that Representative Donald Payne of Pennsylvania would head a six-member U.S. delegation to the inauguration.

In addition to Payne, a Democrat, the U.S. delegation will include Chip Carter, the son of former President Jimmy Carter, and Reps. John Conyers of Michigan and Cynthia McKinney of Georgia, both Democrats.
Also participating will be special presidental envoy Howard Jeter and William Milam, U.S. chief of mission in Monrovia.
Troops of the West African peacekeeeping force ECOMOG and Liberia's rump national army paraded down the streets of central Monrovia, spruced up for the ceremony.
ECOMOG fired a canon at daybreak to flag off festivities.

Taylor led last-minute preparations over the past two days, including redecoration of the inaugural venue -- the Centennial Hall erected in central Monrovia 50 years ago on the 100th anniversary of the founding of Liberia by freed American slaves.

Streets in the the city centre, bustling again after the devastation caused by militia warfare and massive looting in April-May 1996, are festooned with Liberia's national flag -- the Lone Star -- a modest copy of the U.S. Stars and Stripes.
Workers repainted walls of the dilapidated Executive Mansion, the seafront officce and residence presidential complex over which faction leaders fought a bitter seven-year war.
Liberians seeking to close a horrific chapter in their national history opted for strong leadership by voting massively for Taylor -- the man who started the conflict in December 1989.
The widows of Liberia's last two presidents from the descendants of freed slaves -- William Tubman and William Tolbert -- were invited as special guests at the inauguration, organisers said.
Tolbert, the last of the so-called Americo-Liberian presidents, was killed in a 1980 coup led by then sergeant Samuel Doe, who became the last elected president in 1985.
Doe's alleged rigging of those elections precipitated the chain of events leading to the civil war in which he was captured by guerrillas and tortured to death in September 1990.
Taylor will be the first Americo-Liberian leader since 1980.
